generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, evaluation is where you weigh one interpretation against another. A single source rarely settles a question, and rival readings often compete to account for the same evidence. To evaluate is to ask which fits the evidence better, and why: how strong the support is, whether it holds up elsewhere, whether a simpler account would do. The judgement comes with reasons drawn from the evidence, not from preference.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing about the same interpretation of a well-known finding.

{{learner-a}} takes the interpretation apart neatly: here is the claim, here is the source offered for it, here is the reasoning. The account is accurate, and it stops there. {{learner-a}} has analysed the interpretation but not weighed it, and says nothing of how strong it is or how it stands against any other reading of the evidence. This is analysis without evaluation.

{{learner-b}} goes further. Having seen the parts, {{learner-b}} sets this interpretation against a rival one and asks which better accounts for the evidence. The first explains more but rests on thin support; the second is wider but vaguer. {{learner-b}} judges the first stronger on balance, and says why. This is evaluation.

Both students understood the interpretation. Only {{learner-b}} weighed its value against an alternative, with reasons, which is what makes a reading evaluative.
generatedProse.summary: Evaluation means weighing the relative value of an interpretation against alternatives, with reasons drawn from the evidence, rather than judging it in isolation. You can now tell evaluation apart from analysis and choose an evaluative question to ask of a source. The next lesson completes the set: synthesis draws several evaluated sources together into an argument of your own.

check.body: In the worked example, what did {{learner-b}} do that {{learner-a}} did not?

items.text: {{learner-b}} weighed the interpretation against a rival and judged which better fit the evidence, with reasons.
{{learner-b}} separated the interpretation into its claim, evidence and reasoning.
{{learner-b}} quoted the original source more fully.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the interpretation against a rival, with reasons, is evaluation.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. {{learner-a}} had already taken the interpretation apart, so look for what {{learner-b}} added.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} evaluated: weighing the interpretation against an alternative and judging which better fit the evidence, with reasons. Both students had already analysed it.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
